insider_note: Every rectangular hyperbola has eccentricity exactly √2 — this single number is worth remembering as a fact, not just a formula result, since 'find e for a rectangular hyperbola' can be asked with no other numbers given at all.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Definition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The name comes from the asymptotes meeting at a right angle.
steps.memory_tip: Rectangular hyperbola = transverse axis EQUALS conjugate axis, i.e. a = b.
lines: A hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 is called a rectangular hyperbola when its transverse axis and its conjugate axis are equal in length.
Transverse axis = 2a, conjugate axis = 2b, so 2a = 2b ⇒ a = b
steps.why: The name 'rectangular' comes from the asymptotes: when a = b the asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x become y = ±x, which are perpendicular — the two asymptotes meet at a right angle, like the sides of a rectangle.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'rectangular hyperbola' with 'right hyperbola' or some other name — the definition is specifically a = b.
Writing the condition as a² = b² without stating it comes from equal axis LENGTHS 2a = 2b.

steps.label: Eccentricity
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Substitute a = b into the ordinary eccentricity formula.
steps.memory_tip: Every rectangular hyperbola has e = √2, no matter its size.
lines: e = √(a² + b²)/a, and a = b ⇒ e = √(a² + a²)/a = √(2a²)/a
steps.why: Substituting b = a into the ordinary eccentricity formula and cancelling the common factor of a gives a fixed numeric eccentricity — every rectangular hyperbola has the same eccentricity √2, regardless of its size.
common_mistakes: Leaving √(2a²)/a without cancelling the a, instead of simplifying to the pure number √2.
Writing e = 2 instead of √2 by mis-simplifying the square root.
